Design Build Fly

Fall 2024 - Spring 2026

MIT students building RC planes for the AIAA’s design/build/fly competition.

Skills & Tools: CAD (Fusion 360), stability analysis (XFLR5), composite manufacturing, lasercutting, Monokote

Links: [team website]

2026 Competition

For the 2026 competition, our two missions were to carry as large of a banner as possible, and as many ducks and pucks as possible. After realizing that the two missions were in direct conflict, and that fewer ducks and pucks would help us achieve a faster ground mission time, we decided to prioritize banner size, and to carry the minimum required number of ducks and pucks.

Our first prototype prioritized manufacturability. I designed the wing in Fusion 360, sized to an off-the-shelf carbon spar we already had. I laser-cut the ribs and stringers and led manufacturing. We successfully test-flew this prototype and attempted a banner release.

I scaled down the wing and added twist and dihedral to the second prototype wing design for better performance. We made several changes to the fabrication. We laid up the control surface hinges with kevlar. We also attempted a monokote leading edge, instead of the foam cut leading edge we had used previously, but this resulted in an uneven leading edge, so we added a carbon fiber leading edge we laid up. Most importantly, we built a custom spar from balsa and unidirectional carbon fiber, which we spent several weeks perfecting.

Because the control surface horns were not fully secured, and some other issues, we weren't able to successfully test fly our second prototype before building the final aircraft.

For our final aircraft, we kept the same wing design, but perfected our fabrication techniques. We also sized up the tail after we had second thoughts about the second prototype and changed the angle of incidence for better performance when flying with the banner.

We test-flew both our second and final aircraft. The final aircraft performed well; the second had stability issues, which we tried to fix by extending the tail.

At competition, we successfully completed the first two missions (flying 3 laps, and flying with cargo), but weren't able to attempt the third mission (banner) because of a glitch with the transmitter. We finished 29th out of the over 90 teams that attended fly off.

2025 Competition

We built small balsa gliders and larger RC aircraft as part of DBF’s new member training. Our wobbly wing-fuselage attachment caused it to crash.

Our mission requirements for the year’s competition involved creating an autonomous glider that could hit a target, so I helped brainstorm glider configurations. I did some back-of-the-envelope calculations to figure out the lift-drag ratio we’d need.

I helped with fabrication, including monokoting the wing and laying up the tail in fiberglass, for the first test flight.

We had our first test flight at the end of the semester! The plane had no dihedral and an essentially non-existent fuselage, so it was neutrally stable and required attentive piloting. It flew several laps successfully.

We decided to build a glider in the conventional configuration, so I built several gliders with different methods to see what would be lightest. We tried testing the gliders, including by dropping them from a drone, but found that it was difficult to find a reliable way to release the glider.

I wrote the airfoil selection section in our design doc.

I spent a lot of time helping build two more aircraft to test fly, and spare parts to bring to competition to ensure we’d be able to recover from a crash.

At competition, I helped fix last minute problems (like a screw that just wouldn’t come out from a broken motor, and the glider release mechanism that kept sticking) and talked to other teams. Although we didn’t perform as well as I would’ve liked at competition (we were late in the flight order because we accidentally added extra empty pages to our design doc, so we had fewer attempts to fly), I still had fun and learned a lot.

Summer Science Program

Summer 2023

My team observed near earth asteroid 2002 MQ3, reduced images, found right ascension and declination, and determined its orbit using the Method of Gauss.

Skills & Tools: Monte Carlo, image processing, Python, multiprocessing, Method of Gauss

Links: [code] [report]

I wrote several more times code at SSP than I ever have. Much of it was translating equations that we had gone over during lecture into python, which was theoretically simple but very hard to debug.

Least squares plate reduction (LSPR) was the first program we wrote specifically for processing our data. It turns x, y coordinates on a .fits image into right ascensions and declinations using known stars. Compared to the others it wasn’t too complicated; the hardest part was translating the sums into for loops.

Aperture photometry compares the signal of our asteroid to that of known reference stars to find its apparent magnitude. It was difficult because of centroiding — it was riddled with off-by-one errors and difficult to debug because wrong results seemed accurate. I also accidentally swapped x and y when slicing out the region of interest, and spent an hour wondering why my signal was negative, until our TA Kathryn explained. The actual mathematics to calculate signal and noise wasn’t difficult, though I had to be careful when selecting my stars to create the line of best fit; here’s one of my write-ups of the results.

Programming the Method of Gauss to determine our asteroid’s orbit started with a long pseudocode, then extensive debugging. In my first few attempts I converted from Gaussian time into regular time at the wrong step, which resulted in my orbital elements being slightly off and my f & g functions not working for some inputs. Our asteroid converged after over 60 iterations (which would be really, really annoying to have to calculate by hand).

After writing the Method of Gauss, I attempted orbit improvement, which was actually successful as it decreased the root mean square of the predicted orbit — interesting, since the other group observing 2002 MQ3 didn’t find orbit improvement helpful. I also chose to use multiprocessing via Python’s multiprocessing library to create a monte carlo program estimating the error on our orbital elements given the error on our original right ascensions and declinations. With 1 million runs, I got some nice bell curves of each of the orbital elements.

Flight Club Aerospace

Spring 2021 - Spring 2024

A group of about twenty high schoolers designing and building a pt. 103 ultralight aircraft! In my 3.5 years on the team as a design team member, and later, design co-lead, I worked on the design of a part 107 ultralight and the design and fabrication of a 12’ wingspan prototype.

Skills & Tools: CAD (Fusion 360), stability analysis (XFLR5), FEA (Fusion 360), CFD (Simscale, Paraview)

Links: [website]

2021

I was immediately tasked with simulating the fuselage for a full scale pt. 103 ultralight in Fusion 360’s FEA program. We started with simulations of lift at cruise (my notes on the forces), and went onto simulating forces on every part of the fuselage. Experimenting with Fusion simulation’s features — especially solving our last few simulations without constraints in rigid body mode — taught me a lot about breaking down forces and finding global equilibrium.

Our fuselage CAD was not perfect and the program had a tendency to fail meshing — runtimes were around five hours per simulation when they did work — so we had some strange workarounds, including putting spheres on the joints and removing most of the crossmembers from the simulation. The simulations showed us that we needed to push the beams at the bottom of the cabin backward to create a strong attachment for the aft spar.

Through the process we realized that our center of gravity was too far aft, which would make our plane unstable. We tried to remedy this by elongating the nose, but that didn’t fix the issue as much as we had hoped, opening up debate over switching to an aluminum fuselage, which would be lighter than the 4130 chromoly steel we had originally intended to weld.

Towards the end of March we met with Professor Jeff Hasson of Texas Tech, who suggested a few tweaks to the back of the cabin and doing simulations of roll forces, but otherwise approved our design. Professor Shirmohamadi also advised us on testing the wing attachment.

Overall, the process taught me to trust common sense before attempting to run something through a simulation — it’s faster that way.

Come summer, I started attending fabrication and learning shop skills — my first time doing so — mainly by building the wing. I enjoyed it, but design still remains my expertise.

After being elected Design Co-Lead, I led a subteam on control systems, designing the bellcranks for the rudder and elevator and researching cable strength. I also helped design the aileron bellcrank, doing some geometry so the aileron would go up more than down, and making a cardboard mock-up after the math got confusing.

We double checked our fuselage strength using a skewer and hot glue model, per the advice of some builders on the homebuilt airplanes forum — it worked! Moral of the story for both control systems and the fuselage: when in doubt, mock it up!

For the rest of summer I finished up small projects — designing braking for the landing gear, finalizing CG and pilot placement, and selecting a ballistic recovery system. We also redesigned the tail to improve static stability using XFLR5, which taught me about moments and aerodynamic coefficients. I did tail volume coefficient calculations to do a gut check on XLFR5’s results. We decided on a negative camber airfoil which was not ideal, but kept the tail reasonably sized.

I cozied up to the General Aviation Aircraft Design textbook to estimate drag so we could spec the motor.

After training new recruits, I worked on the landing gear, namely calculating the force of impact to choose a spring. We didn’t finish, because in mid-August we met with Jump Aero, who told us that our front spars would probably break at high angles of attack. After a lot of heated debate, we decided to switch to designing a subscale prototype, which meant redoing our XFLR5 simulations and adjusting the tail size. I found that Reynolds scaling was impractical and got advice from Sanchit from Elroy Air to scale inertially. We decided on a model of about ⅙ mass, with wingspan ⅓ of our intended ultralight.

We continued discussing our design with Elroy Air, and switched from a cloth-covered wing to foam ribs with fiberglass. Justin from Elroy Air advised us on how to lay the fiberglass, and how to use a hot wire cutter to cut the foam into molds.

I led a subteam on CFD simulations to corroborate XFLR5 — something I only had an old blog post to help me with. After digging through forums, I learned how to visualize case files from SimScale in Paraview, then sliced them to get CSVs at one cross section of the wing with lift at each point. I fitted the data to a polynomial curve using some code, and created a desmos of chordwise lift distribution at different angles of attack.

Meanwhile we bought and tested several spars. I calculated some test cases using the Schrenk approximation and helped on one of our first successful tests.

At the end of the year, Nisu and I went to CNC the gussets for the spar at Kyle’s machine shop. He showed me how to use the Kitamura CNC — super cool!

2022

We began testing the new fiberglass wing design. I helped route the ribs and wrap them in fiberglass, then used my CFD chordwise lift distributions to design tests for rib strength — the rib held!

We also made our own hot wire cutter and cut foam molds, which was more difficult than expected because the long nichrome wire sagged, leading to wavy cuts. Our workaround was cutting using positive templates, over multiple passes.

The test wing’s fiberglass sagged between the ribs. We tried adding a bulkhead and a top hat, neither of which worked, so we increased the number of ribs and looped the fiberglass over the front edge.

Design finished up the remaining projects. I helped design the landing gear, mainly estimating forces. We used a carbon fiber leaf spring for the main gear, but the leaf spring for the front gear never arrived, so we built a rigid landing gear from square tubing instead.

For most of the spring I tried unsuccessfully to build a model of our plane in Gazebo. Our software lead eventually created one on a virtual machine, but it kept tilting inexplicably. I was able to get the model with joints working on a Mac, but the code for aerodynamic characteristics wouldn’t compile — there was an error with qmake that I tried running by Fischer and Karan from Elroy Air, but none of their solutions or the ones on stack overflow worked.

In preparation for the flight, I calculated our v-speeds and found them to be high but feasible.

Leading up to the flight, Flight Club Aerospace focused entirely on fabrication. With the design finished, I helped build the fuselage and tail. We did taxi testing in Alameda on July 4. Our plane hit a pothole and tipped over, shattering the propeller and twisting the front landing gear. Thankfully, almost everything else was undamaged, so we were able to fix the landing gear, get a new propeller, and head to El Mirage Dry Lake for the test flight.

We first attempted a hop. The plane became airborne, but it landed too hard and the front landing gear collapsed. We weren’t able to fix the landing gear completely, so the plane wasn’t able to surpass stall speed on the ground. Our pilot tried a soft field takeoff, but the plane took off too early, stalled, and crashed. At which point we were out of spare propellers.

We took a break after the test flight — most of us were traveling or, in my case, sick.

Besides redesigning the front landing gear to be solid piping with rubber shock absorbers, we also decided to extend the fuselage for more tail control. We redid XFLR5 simulations, deciding on a nearly twice as long fuselage for better static and dynamic stability, which I CADed. We also decided to redo the leading edge of our wings.

After training the year’s recruits, I led a team to calculate the dimensions of the new strut and verify the strength of the spar. We self-studied statics using Jeff Hanson’s videos and made a Desmos calculator after locking ourselves in a library conference room to grind through the calculations for a few hours. We also checked the strength of two fuselage beams that would be taking the force of the main landing gear and the pull of the struts.

We designed the gussets for the fuselage, and got really good at sketching and using the sheet metal tool. Tedious stuff, but necessary.

2023

I led a team to redesign the control systems; I designed the system for the elevator, using Fusion’s sheet metal tool yet again. Though not the failure point during the first flight, they weren’t as strong as they should have been, and we wanted to make them more lightweight.

Flight Club’s focus switched to fabrication for the second half of the spring, so I concentrated on training design members in CFD using SimScale and helping them become more confident with CAD with CAD challenges (I had a lot of fun helping Jay and Gracie piece together the twist strip challenge).

I fixed some last-minute problems as they came up, including redesigning the battery mount to be more secure, and fixing the rudder control system, which had an impossible-to-cut gusset.

Because I attended SSP, I wasn’t able to attend the test flight. The plane crashed into a tent; it’s suspected that one of the control linkages broke, perhaps in addition to some lag in the system, but because the plane is almost completely destroyed no one’s sure what the failure was.

Without a space to work out of, I focused on training new members and piecing together what happened during the flight. We decided to keep the same aircraft design, but improve fabrication techniques for a more reliable plane. We researched techniques to lay fiberglass as the leading edges on our previous wings sagged between the ribs. We also researched better hot wire cutter designs, eventually deciding on a design tensioned by weights, to ensure our molds would be even.

NASA Techrise

Summer 2022 - Fall 2023

A six-person team of Aragon students who won the NASA TechRise Challenge. We’ve designed, built, and launched an experiment that monitors the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide catalyzed by potassium iodide in microgravity.

Skills & Tools: CAD (Onshape), testing and troubleshooting, soldering

Links: [website]

We brainstormed many ideas for a proposal, then ranked each based on the competition criteria. I did an experiment in my AP Biology class observing the efficacy of catalase under different temperatures and pH levels, so I suggested we do a similar experiment in microgravity, which was the idea we chose to use. We ran a version of the experiment to see how it might work, and decided to use resistance to measure how much oxygen gas was being produced. We CADed a design with two syringes and a reaction chamber and submitted our proposal.

After we learned that we won, we immediately started talking to teachers about polishing our experiment. Ms. Ward, the AP Biology teacher, brought to our attention that catalase was not shelf stable. We looked into ways to stabilize the enzyme, including adding glucose and glycerol, since the experiment would be in storage for months before the launch. We tried adding glycerol to catalase and leaving it at room temperature, but the catalase degraded, so we switched to potassium iodide.

Our chemistry teacher Mr. Doyle recommended that we measure volume and pressure in order to calculate the amount of oxygen, rather than resistance, which would be affected by ions generated during the reaction. He demonstrated to us the upside down burette method, then we did our own version of the experiment using potassium iodide and hydrogen peroxide with the help of Mr. Moretti. I did the stoichiometric calculations to see how much hydrogen peroxide we should use, and researched the Van Der Waals equation and Henry’s law to derive equations to calculate the total amount of oxygen produced.

We went through several iterations of the design: a syringe and a large reaction chamber and two syringes with a test tube before deciding to use two syringes, the larger one carrying hydrogen peroxide and serving as the reaction chamber, and the smaller carrying potassium iodide. We built it — and then struggled to make it leak proof. After unsuccessfully trying caulking, our NASA mentors introduced us to Luer Locks, and Mr. Apperson, our shop teacher, showed us PTFE tape. We conducted lots of tests until the experiment stopped leaking. At the end of it I learned to iterate, iterate, iterate. We failed. Many times.

We 3D printed our mount out of PETG. I tried a clamp design originally, but we settled for zip ties that Jorell designed. Designing the tolerances was a struggle because PETG does not print cleanly — at one point Jorell used a blow torch and screwdriver to widen the zip tie slots.

As our electronics arrived, we started testing and designing the mechanism to depress the small syringe. We tried a push-pull bar and even considered a four bar linkage before I designed a screw gear. However, the bevel gears that connected the stepper to the stepper motor kept skipping teeth and the motor did not have enough torque.

By the end of the school year, we had a mostly working prototype. We continued to test for leaks, and strength tested our setup by putting everything together and throwing it around (unfortunately, our mount just barely didn’t fit inside the flight box). Meanwhile we noticed that the hydrogen peroxide was corroding our brass NPT fittings and our solenoid valve.

Rachel worked on the code, and Jake soldered, so by the end of the summer, our sensors were working as well.

We printed our final mount, finally got everything to fit inside, and staked and potted our electronics. We tried to fix the corrosion on the NPT fittings by coating them with polyurethane, which didn’t work, so we switched to plastic NPT fittings. We couldn’t find a plastic solenoid, so we left an air gap between the hydrogen peroxide and the solenoid.

We got a DC motor with more torque and fixed our screw gear, removing the bevel. A little bit of graphite to lubricate and it worked!

The last few weeks were focused on soldering, testing, and screwing everything together — including last minute runs to Ace Hardware when we realized a screw was missing. Thankfully the switch to plastic NPT fittings left us nicely under the 500g limit. We shipped October 19.

Our experiment launched on Blue Origin's New Shepard late 2025. Unfortunately, it didn't work as expected (we suspect that after several years in storage, the hydrogen peroxide degraded).

Nasa Ames Unitary Plan Wind Tunnel Internship

Summer 2025

Characterizing the uncertainty in a stereophotogrammetry system used by the NASA Ames Unitary Plan Wind Tunnel to measure model angle of attack. Mentored by Ted Garbeff and Lindsey Drone.

Skills & Tools: stereophotogrammetry, OpenCV, Python multiprocessing, Monte Carlo, uncertainty analysis

Links: [final presentation]

(some of the interns in IR)

Most commercial and military aircraft built in the US have small-scale models tested in the NASA Ames Unitary Plan Wind Tunnels. Accurate tests require knowing the model's position, especially its angle of attack. Accelerometers inside the model aren't reliable because they can't take accurate readings when vibrating. The current angle measurement system relies on an angle sensor mounted at the base of the structure supporting the model to avoid vibrations. Because of the slop in the system, this measurements requires corrections that have to be calibrated for every model, and this is a long process.

One of my mentors had been working on a camera-based pose estimation system that would avoid the vibration and calibration issues. I was tasked with determining the uncertainty in this system.

I started by getting familiar with Ted’s camera and light setup, the hexapod (a platform with 6 degrees of freedom and 0.00001mm accuracy) and OpenCV in Python. I spent some time blazing through computer vision textbooks — I hadn’t done anything with computer vision before, so I had to learn a lot.

I wrote a suite of detection and refinement methods using OpenCV’s functions: blob detection, Harris corner detection, convolution, and ellipse fit refinement, centroiding, corner refinement, and a special convolution refinement algorithm Ted devised. I wrote methods to triangulate points and convert from the camera reference frame to the hexapod’s. I also experimented with camera calibration — and realized that it was far finickier than expected.

The other interns and I about a dozen targets of different shapes and sizes with an airbrush and Cricut stencils. I started taking my own data. I did experiments to determine the system’s accuracy in measuring motion of a few mm with different targets.

I realized that to get a better picture of the error in the system, I wanted a lot of precise data points, that I could take quickly. So I used different calibration boards (checker pattern and dot pattern) and measured the positions of the dots relative to each other with the cameras, then compared the results to the board’s specs. I found that the accuracy depended a lot on the calibration I used, and that errors were systematic (some parts of the board all skewing one way, for example) so I used multiple pictures of the same board in the exact same position to determine error from noise, and then dived deeper into calibration.

I took several thousand photos of a checker calibration board in different positions and used that as the raw data to run a Monte Carlo simulation on camera calibration. Combining that with the measured error from noise, I input all the errors into a Monte Carlo simulation on triangulation, and found that error in camera calibration had the largest effect on error in triangulation results.

I did other experimenting to see the effects of other possible variables: like vibration (I convinced two test engineers, the interns, and Lindsey to jump up and down in sync with me in the lab), binning, and lighting.

The presentation I gave to the NASA Ames Aeronautics division at the end of my internship. It had cooler animations in powerpoint.

I spent a fair amount of time making sure that the code I wrote was well documented, in the hopes that it’ll be used in the future (because it’s free! and matlab isn’t!). I used multiprocessing with the detection methods so I could process many images in parallel, speeding up my data analysis (the images were each ~50mb, so any speedup helped a lot). I also optimized the original convolution refinement code I wrote to take advantage of arrays, finally getting it to similar speeds as OpenCV’s other detection / refinement methods.

Despite this, my poor intern loaner laptop hit 100% CPU frequently. During some Monte Carlo runs (camera calibration, ahem), I left it running for a few hours to go explore other NASA labs or the wind tunnels!

Cool things I got to see (that I’m allowed to post):

  • Schlieren (shadowgraph) — we popped balloons and played a trumpet and watched the sound waves with a high speed camera
  • the Vertical Gun Range, which I wouldn’t describe as a gun but more like a cannon that simulates asteroid impacts, capsules descending, etc.
  • the super computing facility
  • the largest wind tunnel in the world
  • an anechoic RF chamber
  • the lead screw that adjusts the floor of the wind tunnel, changing its mach number

I also had time to take cool photos with the wind tunnel’s IR camera and make a 3D music video using the camera setup (see the end of the presentation!).

Oystermaran

Fall 2024 - Spring 2025

I designed PCBs for and troubleshot the electrical system of a robotic boat.

Skills & Tools: KiCAD, PCB layout, milling, solder masking, and assembling, PWM, electrical troubleshooting

Links: [website]

Oysters are grown in strings of baskets. Each basket is approximately 2ft by 3ft, and can weigh up to 50 lbs when filled with fully grown oysters. The baskets need to be flipped regularly because algae grows on the bottom and suffocates the oysters. Currently, the only way to flip them is for someone to go out on a kayak and flip the baskets one by one. No one really likes doing this.

Oystermaran is a robotic boat that, when finished, will autonomously flip the oyster baskets.

I learned KiCAD and designed a simple PCB for Flippy to connect signals from the Pixhawk and Raspberry Pi, replacing the previous protoboard. I routed the traces by hand to ensure the PCB was one-sided, since we wanted to manufacture the PCB on-site. I learned how to use an Othermill, milled the PCB (several times, because I got it wrong a lot!), then soldermasked and soldered it.

I helped debug the electronics system, allowing us to complete a test in Sea Grant's tank.

I designed a mount to hold the Pixhawk, GPS, PCB, Raspberry Pi, battery terminals, and other electronics within a waterproof box. I lasercut the mount and other metal parts, on a Fablight.

I experimented with using an I2C breakout board from Adafruit to control servos, and designed yet another PCB that integrated the I2C breakout. We ordered them from PCBway; I soldered and installed one onto Flippy.

Tasan Group

Fall 2025

I finetuned Mistral 7B instruct to give feedback on clarity and conciseness for first drafts of scientific manuscripts.

Skills & Tools: Huggingface, Pytorch, finetuning, LLMs

Links: [presentation]

Professor Taşan leads the Taşan Group, which produces many papers per month. Giving feedback, especially on early drafts where the focus is on clarity and concision, is time-consuming. The group wanted to try using LLMs to get initial feedback, but can't use online models like ChatGPT because of data privacy concerns. I fine-tuned an LLM based on feedback Professor Taşan gave to prior papers.

Since the model had to be run locally, I was restricted in the size of the model I could use. Therefore I chose Mistral 7B instruct, a relatively small pre-trained LLM that performed well on creative writing and reasoning tasks.

I collected papers and feedback, trying to find a variety of papers (both those targeting high-impact journals like Nature and those written for field-specific papers like Acta Materialia) with a variety of feedback. Since feedback often was in the form of direct edits, but we wanted to train the LLM to provide commentary rather than returning a rewritten version of the paper, this often involved speaking to the authors to understand the reasoning behind changes. In all, I gathered about ten thousand words of papers and commentary, which I manually divided into pairs of paper sections and the corresponding commentary to speed up training.

I wrote a training script with Pytorch and Huggingface tools, and started training. Because of the small dataset, I found that after several epochs the model tended to return the same feedback for every input: "the sentence is too long and wordy." I implemented early stopping to fix this issue.

As a relatively small large language model, my fine-tuned version of Mistral 7b Instruct performed fairly well. Because the majority of the feedback on the papers I collected was about conciseness, much of the feedback returned by Mistral 7b Instruct focused on this too. However, as a final gut-check, I tested Mistral 7b Instruct on drafts not seen during training, and showed the feedback to the authors; they found that the feedback generally made sense, and the suggestions were helpful. There were some hallucinations and some comments that didn't make sense, but it was helpful for a first pass.

MIT MRL

Spring 2026

I developed a machine learning tool to match researchers at MIT with companies interested in sponsoring research.

Skills & Tools: Spacy, sentence transformers, keyword embedding, querying APIs

Links: [github]

MRL supports large, interdisciplinary materials-related projects at MIT. Given the current research funding climate, MRL has been focusing on attracting and retaining industry funding.

There are many companies interested in sponsoring research, but they often don't know where to start. Who are the experts in the field? What are their current research interests? Are the relevant recent innovations? With over a thousand PIs at MIT, these questions become difficult for any one person to answer. The problem only compounds when you look at academia as a whole.

I developed a tool that gathers public data about MIT research and company interests in order to finds matches between researchers and companies.

Specifically, there are three steps: gathering data, embedding the data, and computing matches.

For PIs, I gather their papers from OpenAlex and generate general keywords describing their research from Gemini. For companies, I search recent job listings on Indeed, papers from OpenAlex, US patents, and general keywords from Gemini.

For job listings and patents, I extract materials-science related key words from the descriptions using Spacy with the sentence transformer all-mpnet-base-v2. Then I embed the extracted keywords and paper titles using the same model, and calculated a score based on recency of data and relevance of the source. Everything then went into a Sqlite3 database.

To generate matches, I used the sum of the cosine similarities between a company's keywords and a researcher's keywords, weighed by the keywords' scores to determine a match score.

Some not-so-surprising results: the highest match scores were in researcher-company pairs where the researcher had already written a paper sponsored by the company. Some of the high-scoring matches were obvious — a metallurgy professor with Tata Steel, for example, but others were less so — a civil engineering professor with Raytheon, who showed interested in topology optimization for heat transfer, exactly the area she was trying to steer her lab towards.

While I was working on this project, MRL was kickstarting several pilot centers — multi-company collaborations centered around one PI. I used this tool to suggest initial companies for the PIs to reach out to, and when some companies came wanting to fund several projects, I also searched for appropriate PIs at MIT to contact.
